captions: Part one. Why agents need memory at all.
Couldn't we just use a bigger context window?
The simplest memory is no memory system at
all. Just replay the whole conversation, every time.
It works, and it's actually the accuracy ceiling
in the Mem0 paper.
But look at the cost. On the LoCoMo
benchmark, the full conversation averages about twenty six
thousand tokens per question.
Mem0 puts about seventeen hundred tokens of memories
into context instead. Its graph variant, about thirty
six hundred.
And conversations only grow. Replay scales with everything
ever said. Memory scales with what actually matters.
So the trade-off looks like this.
Replaying everything means cost and latency grow with
every turn. Long contexts also bury details in
the middle, where models pay less attention. And
a new session starts empty anyway.
A memory layer distills facts once, stores them
outside the model, and retrieves only what's relevant,
so the context per question stays roughly constant.
That's the whole bet: pay a little at
write time, to save a lot at read
time.
It helps to borrow from cognitive science.
Working memory is the context window itself: small
and fast.
Episodic memory records what happened, and when, like
the trip to Goa last March.
Semantic memory holds stable facts and preferences: the
user is vegetarian, and prefers Python.
Procedural memory is know-how: routines an agent has
learned for doing a task.
Mem0 mostly manages the middle two, and it
also offers a procedural mode that summarizes an
agent's execution history.
Mem0 isn't the only design.
MemGPT, now called Letta, treats the context window
like an operating system treats RAM, and lets
the agent page memories in and out with
its own function calls.
Zep builds a temporal knowledge graph.
A-Mem organizes memories as linked, self-evolving notes.
LangMem is LangChain's memory toolkit.
And plain RAG simply chunks old conversations and
retrieves raw text.
The Mem0 paper benchmarks against all of these,
and we'll see how they compare in part
seven.
